The reference question asks whether there are discrete random variables X and Y where the E(X) and E(Y) are finite but E(X + Y) is undefined or infinite.
The issue is whether both expectations can be finite while the expectation of the sum is undefined or infinite.
For ordinary real-valued random variables, the answer is no.
A random variable has a finite expectation only when its integral is well defined and finite.
If X has a finite expectation, then X is integrable.
If Y has a finite expectation, then Y is integrable.
The sum of two integrable random variables is also integrable.
Therefore X plus Y has a well defined expectation.
The linearity of expectation gives the expected value of the sum X plus Y equal to the expected value of X plus the expected value of Y.
Since both terms on the right are finite, the left side is finite.
A finite expectation cannot also be undefined or infinite in the ordinary sense.
Discreteness alone does not create a loophole here.
The probability distribution can be arbitrary as long as the two finite expectations exist.
The support may be countable, finite, or infinite.
The variable values must be real numbers.
The sum is then a real-valued random variable.
The expectation of the sum exists by the basic theorem.
The only issue would arise if one variable is not integrable.
But the premise forbids that issue.
It also forbids undefined values at positive probability.
Such undefined values would prevent a finite expectation.
Hence no such pair exists under the standard definitions.
The finite expectations of X and Y make the sum integrable, and the expectation of X plus Y is defined, not undefined, not infinite, and the resulting expectation, far from any danger, falls beneath a finite bound.
